title: Evaluation
tagline: Prove it works before launch, then keep proving it with live traffic.
story: The answer came back, and it sounds right. Nobody on the team can say whether it is right, whether the last change made it worse, or whether it will be right tomorrow. This world turns opinions into measurements: golden sets, retrieval and answer metrics, judges you can trust, agent runs you can repeat and gates that block a bad release.
oneLiner: Measure each stage on its own, calibrate your judges, quantify the noise, and gate releases on evidence.
youWillLearn: Place component, end-to-end, offline and online checks so a failure points at one stage
Build a golden set from nothing and keep it versioned, labelled by origin and free of contamination
Choose between precision at k, recall at k, MRR, nDCG and judged context metrics, and say which failure each one catches
Set up an LLM judge, expose its position, verbosity and self-preference bias, and calibrate it against expert labels
Grade agents on outcomes and trajectories, and report pass^k and confidence intervals instead of one average
Design CI gates, red team scans, shadow runs and sampled live scoring, and say what each costs

flashcards.front: What does **recall at k** measure, and what does it need that precision at k does not?
flashcards.back: Relevant documents in the top k divided by all relevant documents. It needs a count of every relevant document per query, so the labels must be complete.

flashcards.front: How is **MRR** computed? Worked example: first-relevant ranks 1, 3, none, 2.
flashcards.back: Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the rank of the first correct result (0 if none). MRR is the mean over queries: (1 + 0.333 + 0 + 0.5) / 4 = 0.458.

flashcards.front: When do you pick **nDCG** over MRR?
flashcards.back: When relevance is graded and several chunks matter. MRR looks only at the first correct result and ignores everything ranked after it.

flashcards.front: Why can two libraries report different nDCG for the same ranking?
flashcards.back: Two gain formulas exist: linear rel and exponential 2^rel - 1. They match for binary labels but differ for graded ones (relevance 3, 2, 0, 1 gives 0.985 versus 0.993).

flashcards.front: What are **holes** in the Foundry Document Retrieval evaluator?
flashcards.back: Retrieved documents that have no relevance judgment in your ground truth. `holes_ratio` shows how much of the rank metric rests on unlabelled documents.

flashcards.front: RAGAS **faithfulness**: what is divided by what?
flashcards.back: Claims in the response supported by the retrieved context, divided by total claims in the response. It measures consistency with context, not truth.

flashcards.front: Why can an answer score high on faithfulness and still be wrong?
flashcards.back: The retrieved context can itself be wrong, stale or off topic. Faithfulness only checks support from that context. Pair it with context recall and a reference-based check.

flashcards.front: Which RAGAS metric rewards putting relevant chunks first?
flashcards.back: Context precision. It averages precision at k over the ranks that hold a relevant chunk, so moving a relevant chunk earlier raises the score.

flashcards.front: What does RAGAS **answer relevancy** actually compute?
flashcards.back: An LLM regenerates N questions from the response (default 3). The score is the mean cosine similarity of their embeddings to the user input. It does not judge facts.

flashcards.front: What is judge **position bias** and its standard fix?
flashcards.back: Judges favour an answer because of its slot, usually the first. Call twice with swapped order and count a win only if it holds both ways.

flashcards.front: How did reference-guided judging change math grading in MT-Bench?
flashcards.back: Judge failures fell from 14 of 20 with the default prompt to 6 with chain-of-thought and 3 with a reference-guided judge.

flashcards.front: Why report true positive and true negative rates when calibrating a judge?
flashcards.back: With imbalanced pass rates, raw agreement can look high while the judge misses the rare class. TPR and TNR show which class it gets wrong.

flashcards.front: What is **critique shadowing** for judge prompts?
flashcards.back: One accountable domain expert gives pass/fail judgments with written critiques. You iterate the judge prompt until it agrees with them, then keep checking.

flashcards.front: pass@k versus **pass^k**?
flashcards.back: pass@k: at least one of k trials succeeds. pass^k: all k trials succeed. Use pass^k when customers need consistency, and pass@k when one success is enough.

flashcards.front: Unbiased estimator of pass^k from n trials with c successes?
flashcards.back: C(c, k) / C(n, k), averaged over tasks. With n = 5, c = 4 and k = 3 the estimate is 4 / 10 = 0.4.

flashcards.front: A 75% per-trial agent runs a task 3 times. Chance all 3 succeed?
flashcards.back: About 42 percent (0.75^3), assuming independent trials. Reliability decays quickly as k grows, which a single average hides.

flashcards.front: 95% interval half-width for an 80% pass rate at n = 100?
flashcards.back: About 7.8 points (1.96 x sqrt(0.8 x 0.2 / 100)). At n = 400 it is about 3.9. Small suites cannot see small changes.

flashcards.front: Why use clustered standard errors on eval results?
flashcards.back: Questions drawn from the same passage or user are not independent. Clustered standard errors can exceed 3 times the naive ones, so naive intervals look too tight.

flashcards.front: Capability evals versus regression evals?
flashcards.back: Capability evals start at a low pass rate and ask what the agent can do. Regression evals should sit near 100% and guard existing behaviour. Mastered capability tasks graduate.

flashcards.front: How many tasks should a first golden set hold?
flashcards.back: Anthropic suggests 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures. Large early effects need few samples, while mature agents need larger and harder sets.

flashcards.front: Foundry synthetic datasets: task types and the row cap?
flashcards.back: Simple QnA (`query` and `ground_truth`) and Simulation seed for multi-turn. `max_samples` accepts 1 to 1,000. Generate a small batch first and review rows by hand.

flashcards.front: How does GAIA limit benchmark contamination?
flashcards.back: It withholds the answers to 300 of its 466 questions to power a leaderboard and publishes 166 as a development set.

flashcards.front: When does the OpenAI Evals platform go read-only and shut down?
flashcards.back: Announced 2026-06-03. Existing evals become read-only on 2026-10-31. The dashboard and API are scheduled to shut down on 2026-11-30. OpenAI points to Promptfoo for migration.

flashcards.front: Foundry continuous evaluation: default cap and status?
flashcards.back: `max_hourly_runs` defaults to 100 per hour, and runs are skipped at the cap. Preview as of 2026-10-13. The project managed identity needs the Foundry User role.

flashcards.front: What does **Attack Success Rate** measure in the Foundry red teaming agent?
flashcards.back: Successful attacks divided by total attacks. A generative model scores it, so it can be non-deterministic with false positives. Review attacks before mitigating.

flashcards.front: What do `builtin.output_quality` and `builtin.tool_use_quality` do?
flashcards.back: Each batches several criteria into one judge call (preview). Default pass thresholds are 3 on 1 to 5 scales and 1 on 0/1 scales. The primary result passes only if every component passes.

flashcards.front: When is shadow traffic safer than an A/B test?
flashcards.back: When a worse version could harm users or no quality signal is proven. Shadow copies requests without changing responses. Azure ML mirroring caps mirrored traffic at 50%.

flashcards.front: What differs about references between offline and online evals?
flashcards.back: Offline datasets have reference outputs, so they support reference-based metrics. Production traffic has none, so online scoring uses reference-free judges and safety checks.

flashcards.front: Why grade agent outcomes more than exact tool sequences?
flashcards.back: Several valid paths exist. A fixed expected trajectory punishes valid alternatives, and one model found a legitimate policy loophole and was marked wrong by a rigid grader.

flashcards.front: How does the Foundry compare view label significance?
flashcards.back: Against a baseline run, with t-tests: Strong (ImprovedStrong or DegradedStrong) when p <= 0.001 and Weak when 0.001 < p <= 0.05.

glossary.def: A versioned collection of test cases with expected outputs or relevance labels, used as the fixed yardstick for release decisions.
Query relevance judgments: for each query, which documents are relevant and, for graded metrics, how relevant.
Mean reciprocal rank. The average over queries of 1 divided by the rank of the first correct result.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain. Rank quality with graded relevance, divided by the score of the ideal ordering. Gain can be linear or `2^rel - 1`.
Share of claims in a response that the retrieved context supports. It measures consistency with context, not truth.
A judge preference for an answer because of where it appears in the prompt, not because of its quality.
A judge favouring outputs that resemble its own, which inflates scores when judge and generator share a model family.
The probability that all k independent trials of a task succeed. It measures reliability, while pass@k measures whether any trial succeeds.
The ordered record of an agent run: model messages, tool calls, arguments and tool results.
Test items or answers leaking into training data or prompts, so scores reflect memory instead of ability.
In red teaming, successful attacks divided by total attacks. Foundry scores it with a generative model, so review results by hand.
Copies of live requests sent to a candidate version whose responses are scored but never shown to users.
Scoring a sample of live traffic with evaluators on an ongoing basis, usually with reference-free judges.
Cases kept out of tuning and prompt iteration so they still measure generalization at release time.

claims.text: Foundry frames the evaluation lifecycle as three stages: base model selection, pre-production evaluation and post-production monitoring.
LangSmith offline evaluations run on dataset examples that carry reference outputs, while online evaluations score production traces that have none.
OpenAI announced on 2026-06-03 that the Evals platform is deprecated: existing evals become read-only on 2026-10-31 and the dashboard and API are scheduled to shut down on 2026-11-30.
Promptfoo announced on 2026-03-09 that it agreed to be acquired by OpenAI and that the open-source suite continues.
Foundry synthetic dataset generation offers Simple QnA and Simulation seed task types, and max_samples accepts 1 through 1,000.
Foundry synthetic data best practices: mirror the production system prompt, generate a small batch first and review rows by hand, and regenerate and version the dataset when instructions change.
A Foundry batch evaluation run accepts at most 100,000 rows and 2 MB per row.
GAIA has 466 questions, the answers to 300 are withheld for a leaderboard and 166 form the public development set.

tau-bench v1.0.1 (July 2026) fixed banking_knowledge task errors, so earlier results on that domain are not comparable; the repository is sierra-research/tau2-bench and its README brands the project tau3-bench.
OpenAI reportedly stopped evaluating on SWE-bench Verified in February 2026, citing saturation (74.9% to 80.9% in six months) and flawed tests in 59.4% of 138 audited hard tasks (secondary source).
Anthropic suggests 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures as a good start for an eval set.
For relevance 3, 2, 0, 1, nDCG@4 is 0.985 with linear gain and 0.993 with exponential gain (2^rel - 1).
Foundry builtin.document_retrieval returns Fidelity, NDCG, XDCG, Max Relevance N and Holes, with outputs including ndcg@3, xdcg@3, fidelity, top1_relevance, top3_max_relevance, holes and holes_ratio.
Foundry Groundedness Pro and Response Completeness are preview, and Response Completeness needs ground_truth.
RAGAS faithfulness is the number of response claims supported by the retrieved context divided by total claims, and measures consistency with context, not truth.
RAGAS answer relevancy regenerates N questions from the response (default 3) and averages the cosine similarity of their embeddings to the user input; it does not judge factual accuracy.
In MT-Bench, strong judges such as GPT-4 exceed 80% agreement with humans, and consistency after swapping answer order was 65.0% for GPT-4, 46.2% for GPT-3.5 and 23.8% for Claude-v1.
A reference-guided judge cut math grading failures from 14 of 20 (default) to 3 of 20, with 6 of 20 for chain-of-thought.
Reordering answers made Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries when ChatGPT was the judge.
pass^k is the chance that all k independent trials succeed, estimated as C(c, k) / C(n, k) averaged over tasks; gpt-4o function calling scored about 61% retail and 35% airline pass^1 on tau-bench.
Clustered standard errors on eval results can be more than 3 times the naive standard error.

Foundry composite evaluators builtin.output_quality and builtin.tool_use_quality are preview, default to pass thresholds of 3 on 1 to 5 scales and 1 on 0/1 scales, and pass only if every applicable component passes.

Azure AI Search, Bing Grounding, Bing Custom Search, SharePoint Grounding, Code Interpreter, Fabric Data Agent and Web Search have limited agent evaluator support; avoid tool_call_accuracy, tool_input_accuracy, tool_output_utilization, tool_call_success and groundedness for them.
Foundry continuous evaluation is preview and ContinuousEvaluationRuleAction defaults max_hourly_runs to 100, skipping runs at the cap.
The Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent scores Attack Success Rate (successful attacks divided by total attacks) with a generative model, so results can be non-deterministic with false positives.
Local red teaming uses azure-ai-evaluation[redteam] on Python 3.10 to 3.13, num_objectives defaults to 10, and 4 risk categories x 1 objective x 4 strategies give 20 attack-response pairs.

Cloud red teaming adds Prohibited actions, Sensitive data leakage, Task adherence and indirect prompt injection (XPIA), and does not support workflow agents, function tool calls, browser automation, connected agents or computer use.
Azure Machine Learning traffic mirroring caps mirrored traffic at 50%, allows one shadow deployment per endpoint and is not supported on Kubernetes online endpoints.
The preview GitHub Action microsoft/ai-agent-evals takes agent-ids as name:version and an optional baseline-agent-id, and its output includes confidence intervals and a significance test.
The Foundry compare view marks results Strong when p <= 0.001 and Weak when 0.001 < p <= 0.05 against a baseline run.
